newsitem.title: SWEDEN: IMF concerned about Swedish expenditure programme.
newsitem.headline: IMF concerned about Swedish expenditure programme.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Wednesday that the new Swedish expenditure programme, announced in the spring budget bill, raised some concerns.
In a statement it also said that the monetary stance seemed to be well balanced at the moment.

The IMF welcomed the reaffirmation in the spring budget bill of the government's intention to balance the budget in 1998 and, over the medium term, to achieve an average surplus of two percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over the cycle.
"However, the announcement in the spring budget bill of new expenditure programmes raises some concerns," it said.

The likelihood of sustained success of a fiscal correction programme is higher with a larger expenditure reduction component, which directly addresses the factors responsible for the underlying widening of the deficit, it said.

"Also, notwithstanding the planned lowering of expenditure relative to GDP over the medium term, Sweden's very high public expenditure, and tax burden, relative to GDP cannot but discourage the growth and creation of employment opportunities in the private sector," IMF said.
The prospects for growth and employment opportunities would have been enhanced by using additional resources to lower taxes, it said.

Regarding monetary policy, the IMF approved of the central bank's reduction of its key repurchase rate to 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent in 1996 and also of its decision to keep the rate steady since December 17, 1996.
"This mission also agrees that the monetary stance appears at present to be well balanced," it said.

"With projected growth rates envisaged to close the output gap at an appropriately gradual pace, underlying inflation foreseen to remain within the lower half of the target range for inflation and headline CPI projected to be around target in 1998, there may be some scope for further easing."
A stronger crown, a narrowing of the long bond yield spread with Germany or a failure of the expected economic recovery to materialise would strengthen the case for further easing, it said.
Sweden has had a number of successes in dealing with the economic crisis of the early 1990s, including bringing the budget deficit down to 2.5 percent of GDP in 1996 from 12 percent in 1993, it said.
But the country has failed to reduce unemployment, it said. In April unemployment amounted to 8.3 percent, down from 8.4 percent in March but up from 7.5 percent in April last year, the IMF said.
"Structural reforms, especially in the labour market, are essential to the sustainability of the financial stabilisation itself," it said.
